subject: Get G, C (tilde) matrices from `inla.spde2` object

messages.author: 111f458109435bea
messages.subject: Get G, C (tilde) matrices from `inla.spde2` object
parts:
I'm trying to reconcile the notation used in Lindgren et al. 2011 with the elements of an `inla.spde2` object.
Ultimately, I'd like to use Eq 22 in Appendix 3 of LIndgren et al. 2011 to implement a nonstationary model
in a separate software package (Template Model Builder), using covariates for κ and τ. Fixing α = 2,
Equation 22 gives:

Q = τ(κ²Cκ² + κ²G + Gκ² + GC⁻¹G)τ

where κ and τ are diagonal matrices taking the values of κ(sᵢ) and τ(sᵢ) at the mesh node locations. Looking
at the implementation used to find the precision matrix in the R source for the `inla.spde2.precision`, I see

    Q = (D0 %*% (D1 %*% spde$param.inla$M0 %*% D1 +
                 D12 %*% spde$param.inla$M1 +
                 t(spde$param.inla$M1) %*% D12 +
                 spde$param.inla$M2) %*% D0)


It appears then that the different elements are:
  • `D0` is τ, with elements determined by the regression
  • `D1` is κ², also based on a regression specification
  • `D12` is κ² times another diagonal matrix that is determined by the link function?
  • `M0` is C
  • `M1` is G
  • `M2` is GC⁻¹G
I then have two questions:
  • Are these all correct?
  • When is `D12` different from `D1`?
  • Conceptually, why is `D1`/κ² different in the term with `M0` versus `D12` in the term with `M1`?
Sorry if these are covered elsewhere. I've been working on understanding the SPDE approximation for a
while, but it's starting to come together (thanks in part to Haakon Bakka's explainer on the arXiv, which I
found very helpful).

Thank you,

John Best

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Get G, C (tilde) matrices from `inla.spde2` object
parts:
Hi,

to implement your own SPDE models, I would strongly recommend _not_
extracting the matrices from an inla.spde object, since those are tied
to the internal representation of a family of models including alpha
between 0 and 2, oscillating models, and nonstationary models, all as
described in the Lindgren,Rue,Lindström 2011 JRSSB paper. Instead I
would recommend using inla.mesh.fem() to obtain the C, G, G2=GC^-1G
building block matrices directly and build your code around that. You
can of course still use the inla.spde2.matern and inla.spde2.generic
code to draw inspiration from!

That said, your interpretation of what you found in the object/code is correct.
D12 is different from D1 for oscillating (non-Matérn) models; the
basic oscillating model can be parameterised like this
tau^2 (kappa^4 C + 2 kappa^2 gamma G + GC^-1G),
where gamma is > -1.

I've attached the original design document for the inla.spde2 model family.

Finn
